summary:
Goiás stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, federal anti-discrimination provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, and since the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling transphobia is punishable on the same footing as racism. Same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationally, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

Lethal violence against trans people remains a documented feature of the national picture. ANTRA's ninth annual dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, recorded 80 trans and travesti people killed across Brazil in 2025, a fall of about 34% year-on-year, with Brazil ranked first in world rankings; the victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. Goiás accounted for 5 of those 80 national victims. Against a state population of roughly 7.2 million, that is a rate of about 0.69 per million per year, close to 1.8 times the national rate derived from the same year's figures.

The prior year's tally was higher: ANTRA's dossier for 2024, reported on 27 January 2025, recorded 122 trans and travesti killings nationally, 16% below 2023, with five of the victims rights defenders.

Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed in Brazil, including in Goiás. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.

Protection machinery has widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes. Courts have also applied anti-discrimination provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.
tangentialFactors:
Goiás's rate of trans killings relative to its population sits above the national average derived from the same ANTRA 2025 data, so a trans visitor to the state faces a lethality risk that is not merely the national baseline.

The national trend is downward: 122 trans and travesti killings in 2024 fell to 80 in 2025, a drop of about 34%, though Brazil remains first in world rankings for such homicides and the victims are overwhelmingly travestis and trans women killed with extreme violence.

Drink-spiking robberies targeting LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo nightlife, documented in May 2024, indicate a venue-level predation risk in Brazil's largest city that a trans visitor elsewhere in the country may reasonably treat as a comparable pattern rather than an isolated local hazard.

Trans candidates in the October 2024 municipal elections across every state received death threats and intimidation even as the number of trans officeholders tripled, evidence that visibility in public life carries a specific security cost.
localsOnly:
Residents of Goiás are covered by National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, which lets a person be recognised as LGBTI for prison-placement purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing, and requires the judge to consult the person's preference among male, female and LGBTI-specific units and, within that, the general population or a specific wing or cell.

The same resolutions bar the use of LGBTI-specific living spaces as disciplinary isolation and prohibit compulsory transfer as punishment, and they prioritise transfers where there is violence or a serious threat.

A 2014 federal portaria, reported by G1 on 17 April 2014, granted rights to gay and travesti prisoners including placement in separate accommodation, use of a social name rather than a birth name, forwarding of trans women to women's prisons, and the right to choose male or female clothing. No instrument more recent than that portaria is cited in the sources reviewed for these specific rules.

Lower courts have pressed the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, per a 2022 case-law analysis, bringing trans residents within Brazil's violence-prevention statutes.

Legal gender change in Goiás requires no surgery, following the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2018 removal of the surgical requirement, and gender-marker rules operate on the same basis as elsewhere in Brazil.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Wikipedia article 'LGBTQ people in prison', read in full on 4 October 2026, contains no Brazil-specific trans-prisoner placement rule in its Transgender issues section, discussing only social vulnerability, stigma and fragmented identity of travestis and transgender people during rehabilitation. Whether this reflects an absence of such a rule or simply an omission in that article is unresolved; the National Council of Justice resolutions cited above do govern placement, so the article's silence is best read as scope rather than contradiction.

No Goiás-specific instrument on trans-prisoner placement, hate-crime enforcement, or document rules was located in the sources reviewed; state-level application of the national framework in Goiás courts and prisons is not sourced here.

The 2025 Goiás figure of 5 trans and travesti killings is drawn from ANTRA's national dossier as reported in the press; the underlying state-level methodology, including how victims are counted and verified in Goiás, is not detailed in the sources reviewed.
